case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal court that stays a case pending arbitration retains subject matter jurisdiction to decide post-arbitration motions in that same pending case without identifying a new and independent basis for original jurisdiction.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act, 9 U.S.C. §§ 1-16; 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) (supplemental jurisdiction); 28 U.S.C. § 1254(1) (Supreme Court certiorari jurisdiction)
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner Adrian Jules argues that once a federal court properly establishes original jurisdiction and stays a case pending arbitration, that jurisdiction continuously and automatically extends to post-arbitration motions in the same pending case without requiring the parties to identify a new, redundant, or independent jurisdictional basis. Petitioner further contends that eight circuits have already resolved this question, creating sufficient circuit percolation to warrant Supreme Court review, and that the decision below by the Second Circuit was legally incorrect. Petitioner also asserts that alternative arguments made below regarding vacatur of the arbitration award were procedurally proper under Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(d)(2)-(3) and should not constitute a vehicle problem barring review.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents Andre Balazs Properties et al. argue that the circuit split on this jurisdictional question is weak, shallow, and insufficiently developed to warrant immediate Supreme Court intervention, urging further percolation in the lower courts. Respondents contend that the case presents unique factual circumstances making it a poor vehicle for resolving the broader legal question, and that concerns about forum-shopping and litigation inefficiencies raised by Petitioner are speculative and not grounded in real-world practicalities. Respondents also argue that the Second Circuit's unpublished decision was correct and that the district court properly confirmed the arbitration award after finding no statutory or non-statutory grounds for vacatur under FAA Section 10.
key_precedents: Beijing Shougang Mining Inv. Co. v. Mongolia, 11 F.4th 144, 158 (2d Cir. 2021) — standard of review for arbitration award confirmation (de novo for legal conclusions, clear error for factual findings)
Smarter Tools Inc. v. Chongqing SENCI Imp. & Exp. Trade Co., 57 F.4th 372, 378 (2d Cir. 2023) — heavy burden standard for vacating arbitration awards under FAA Section 10
MasterCard Int'l Inc. v. Visa Int'l Serv. Ass'n, 471 F.3d 377, 382-83 (2d Cir. 2006) — cited regarding proper circumstances for court consideration of arbitration award confirmation
Weiss v. Sallie Mae, Inc., 939 F.3d 105, 109 (2d Cir. 2019) — arbitral decisions construing or applying a contract must stand regardless of court's view of demerits
Publicola v. Lomenzo, 54 F.4th 108, 111 (2d Cir. 2022) — liberal construction of pro se litigant papers
Kotler v. Jubert, 986 F.3d 147, 156 (2d Cir. 2021) — special solicitude for pro se litigants to protect against inadvertent forfeiture of rights
Triestman v. Fed. Bureau of Prisons, 470 F.3d 471, 477 (2d Cir. 2006) — pro se status does not exempt compliance with procedural and substantive law
United Ass'n of Journeymen, Local Union No. 2, 841 F.2d 461, 466-67 (2d Cir. 1988) — cited regarding circumstances for court consideration of arbitration matters
Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(d)(2)-(3) — authorization for alternative and inconsistent pleadings and arguments

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has substantially clarified my thinking. Justice Thomas's textualist challenge remains the most serious — that Badgerow's holding that §§ 9 and 10 require independent jurisdictional bases applies regardless of procedural posture — but as Justice Barrett's methodological consistency point demonstrates most sharply, this argument proves too much: no one contends that courts lose jurisdiction over mid-arbitration motions under §§ 5 and 7, and there is no principled textual basis for treating post-award motions differently when the underlying action remains continuously pending under a mandatory § 3 stay. Justice Kavanaugh's movement toward the Petitioner's position, conditioned on a narrow holding, confirms my instinct that the opinion should be carefully cabined: I would hold only that where a federal court properly established original jurisdiction and issued a mandatory § 3 stay, it retains jurisdiction to resolve post-arbitration FAA motions within that same stayed proceeding, expressly reserving Badgerow's governance of standalone petitions. As opinion-assigning Chief Justice, I would write this majority myself to ensure the holding is sufficiently narrow to command a strong majority while preserving Badgerow's core application to freestanding petitions — a 9-0 or 8-1 result on these precise facts would best serve the institutional legitimacy concerns that animate my judicial philosophy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett's methodological consistency argument has genuinely moved me: if I accept — as everyone does — that courts retain jurisdiction over mid-arbitration motions under Sections 5 and 7 within a stayed case, I cannot coherently maintain that jurisdiction evaporates at award issuance without identifying a textual trigger for that evaporation, and none exists in the FAA's text. Justice Gorsuch's invocation of Kokkonen's ancillary jurisdiction doctrine is also persuasive from an originalist standpoint — the First Judiciary Act tradition I relied upon actually supports inherent power to resolve matters entwined with a pending proceeding, which a post-arbitration motion in a stayed case plainly is. I remain concerned that Smith v. Spizzirri's 'supervisory role' language is statutory interpretation of § 3's mandatory stay requirement rather than an independent jurisdictional grant, and I would write separately to emphasize that this holding must be cabined to cases where original jurisdiction was properly established and a § 3 stay issued — it cannot be read to expand federal jurisdiction beyond that narrow circumstance. On balance, the textual distinction between Badgerow's freestanding petitions and post-arbitration motions within a continuously pending stayed case is sufficiently grounded in § 3's text ('stay the trial of the action') that I am persuaded to join the Petitioner's position, though narrowly.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most serious challenge — that Badgerow's textualist holding requires independent jurisdictional grounding for §§ 9 and 10 applications regardless of procedural posture — remains unpersuasive because it conflates the question of what jurisdiction attaches to a new action with what jurisdiction persists over a continuously pending case. As Justice Barrett correctly identifies, the methodological consistency problem is fatal to the Respondents' position: if courts retain jurisdiction over mid-arbitration motions under §§ 5 and 7 without anyone demanding fresh jurisdictional authorization, there is no principled textual basis for holding that jurisdiction evaporates precisely when the award issues and the court's supervisory function becomes most consequential. Justice Thomas acknowledges that § 1367's supplemental jurisdiction framework provides genuine textual support for the Petitioner's position, and I would add that Kokkonen's ancillary jurisdiction doctrine — which Justice Gorsuch correctly invokes — further confirms that a court retaining a live case on its docket has recognized authority to resolve matters entwined with that proceeding without a new statutory grant. I would write narrowly, consistent with Justice Roberts's framing, to hold only that where original jurisdiction was properly established and a mandatory § 3 stay issued, the court retains jurisdiction over post-arbitration FAA motions within that same stayed proceeding, expressly reserving the standalone petition question Badgerow already resolved.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious challenge by invoking Badgerow's textualist framework and the principle that federal courts require affirmative statutory grants of jurisdiction — but his argument proves too much. Badgerow itself addressed freestanding petitions filed as new actions, and the Court's own language in that decision preserved the question of what happens when post-arbitration motions arise within a previously-stayed case. As Justice Barrett correctly notes, the text of Section 3 directs the court to 'stay the trial of the action,' not to suspend its own jurisdiction — the action remains pending, and a court retaining a live case on its docket retains jurisdiction over proceedings within that case. Justice Kavanaugh's vehicle concerns and preference for further percolation are understandable from an institutionalist perspective, but the circuit split and the concrete harm to pro se litigants like Petitioner Jules — who would be forced to file duplicative actions to access the very federal forum that compelled their arbitration — counsel resolution now rather than deferral. Smith v. Spizzirri's recognition of a 'supervisory role' over stayed proceedings would be rendered hollow if that supervision evaporated at the precise moment it becomes most consequential: when the award issues and a party seeks to enforce or challenge it.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the strongest counterargument — that Badgerow's textual analysis of Sections 9 and 10 applies regardless of whether a prior federal case exists, because those provisions don't distinguish between freestanding and embedded applications. But this reading proves too much: it would mean a court loses jurisdiction over mid-arbitration motions under Sections 5 and 7 as well, an outcome no one defends. As Justice Barrett correctly identifies, the methodological consistency problem is fatal to the Respondents' position — the jurisdictional vessel created by the original filing and § 3 stay cannot logically evaporate at the precise moment the arbitration concludes. The text of § 3 directs a stay of 'the action,' not a termination of it, and Smith v. Spizzirri's confirmation that stays are mandatory rather than discretionary reinforces that Congress understood the stayed case to remain live and under the court's supervision throughout — including post-award. Justice Kavanaugh's vehicle concerns and percolation argument have some institutional appeal, but the circuit split is real and the legal question is sufficiently developed to resolve now.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most serious challenge — that Badgerow's textualist holding requires an affirmative statutory grant regardless of procedural posture — remains the strongest argument for Respondent, but I find it ultimately unpersuasive for the reasons Justice Barrett articulates with particular clarity: Badgerow was careful to address only freestanding petitions, and its reasoning turned on the absence of any predicate federal proceeding, not on a categorical rule that §§ 9 and 10 can never be resolved within a live pending case. The text of § 3 stays 'the trial of the action' — not the court's jurisdiction over the action — and Smith v. Spizzirri's confirmation that stays are mandatory rather than discretionary reinforces that Congress understood the stayed case to remain a live proceeding under continuous federal supervision. Justice Kagan's point about methodological consistency is also compelling: if no one seriously argues that courts lose jurisdiction over mid-arbitration motions under §§ 5 and 7, the logic that jurisdiction evaporates upon award issuance is a textual anomaly, not a faithful reading of the FAA's integrated structure. I would write narrowly, as Chief Justice Roberts suggests, to hold only that where original jurisdiction was properly established and a § 3 stay issued, the court retains jurisdiction over post-arbitration FAA motions within that same proceeding, expressly reserving Badgerow's standalone-petition context.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas's textualist challenge remains the most serious counterargument — that Badgerow's holding requires independent jurisdictional grounding for §§ 9 and 10 applications regardless of procedural posture, and that a stay order cannot serve as a self-executing jurisdictional reservoir. But I am persuaded by Justice Barrett's methodological consistency point, which I find genuinely compelling: if courts unquestionably retain jurisdiction over mid-arbitration motions under §§ 5 and 7 without requiring fresh jurisdictional grounding, it would be a textual anomaly to hold that jurisdiction evaporates precisely when the arbitration concludes and the court's supervisory role becomes most consequential. Justice Alito's distinction between Badgerow's freestanding standalone petitions and post-arbitration motions in a continuously pending stayed case is textually sound — Badgerow's own language was carefully limited to the former, and Smith v. Spizzirri's confirmation that § 3 stays preserve the case as a live proceeding means the original jurisdictional grant persists over that pending case. I would join a narrow majority opinion limited to cases where original jurisdiction was properly established and the case was stayed rather than dismissed, expressly reserving the standalone petition question that Badgerow governs, which cabins the holding and addresses my remaining institutional concerns about breadth.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious challenge by invoking Badgerow's textualist framework and the First Judiciary Act's tradition of limited federal jurisdiction requiring affirmative statutory grants — but his argument proves too much. Badgerow itself was careful to address only freestanding petitions filed as new actions, and the Court's own reasoning in that case distinguished the Section 4 look-through provision precisely because Sections 9 and 10 applications were being filed independently of any predicate federal proceeding. Where, as here, the district court already established original jurisdiction and the case remains on its docket under a mandatory Section 3 stay confirmed by Smith v. Spizzirri, the post-arbitration motions are not 'new' jurisdictional events requiring fresh statutory authorization — they are proceedings within the same live case, and the ordinary rule that a court retaining a case retains jurisdiction over all proceedings in that case is itself a well-established principle of federal practice, not a judicial invention. Justice Kavanaugh's vehicle concerns about the unpublished opinion and circuit-split depth are procedurally prudent but do not undermine the merits analysis, and the anomaly he identifies regarding the maritime exception actually cuts the other way — Congress's express carve-out for maritime cases would be superfluous surplusage if stayed cases never created jurisdictional continuity in the first place, suggesting Congress understood and accepted the general principle.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most serious challenge — that Badgerow's textualist holding requires independent jurisdictional grounding for §§ 9 and 10 regardless of procedural posture — remains the strongest counterargument, but I am further persuaded by Justice Barrett's methodological consistency point that if jurisdiction persists for mid-arbitration motions under §§ 5 and 7, it cannot logically evaporate at the moment the award issues and the court's supervisory role becomes most consequential. Justice Thomas acknowledges that § 1367's supplemental jurisdiction framework provides genuine textual merit for the Petitioner's position, which combined with Smith v. Spizzirri's confirmation that the stayed action remains live on the docket, demonstrates that the court's original jurisdictional grant persists without requiring fresh statutory authorization. Justice Kavanaugh's movement toward the Petitioner's position, conditioned on a narrow holding limited to cases where original jurisdiction was properly established and a § 3 stay issued rather than dismissal, reflects sound institutionalist reasoning that I fully embrace — the holding should be cabined precisely to avoid the broader implications Justice Thomas fears about judicial expansion of federal jurisdiction. My background as a public defender reinforces that the duplicative litigation burden imposed by requiring pro se litigants like Petitioner Jules to re-establish jurisdiction in a new proceeding falls hardest on those least equipped to navigate it, and procedural fairness demands we not impose formalistic re-establishment requirements on parties already in a properly-pending federal case.

John Roberts.reasoning: When a federal court properly establishes original jurisdiction and stays a case pending arbitration under 9 U.S.C. § 3, the case remains pending before that court, and the court retains ancillary jurisdiction to resolve post-arbitration motions without requiring a new independent jurisdictional basis. As this Court held in Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Insurance Co., 511 U.S. 375 (1994), ancillary jurisdiction extends to matters incidental to prior proceedings properly before the court, and the stayed case never left the court's docket — the arbitration award functions analogously to a settlement of the underlying federal claims. Smith v. Spizzirri, 601 U.S. 472 (2024), reinforced that a stay under § 3 keeps the case alive in federal court, which strongly implies the court retains power to act on post-arbitration motions in that same proceeding. Consistent with my preference for narrow rulings, I would hold only that retained jurisdiction in a properly stayed case extends to the entwined post-arbitration FAA motions, without broadly resolving every ancillary jurisdiction question under the FAA.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As an originalist and textualist, I must follow the plain text of the FAA and this Court's authoritative interpretation in Badgerow v. Waters, which held that federal courts must identify an independent jurisdictional basis on the face of a Section 9 or 10 application — the FAA itself confers no subject matter jurisdiction. The text of 9 U.S.C. §§ 9 and 10 does not distinguish between applications filed in pre-existing federal cases and standalone petitions, and nothing in the original public meaning of federal jurisdictional statutes supports the notion that a stayed case creates a perpetual 'jurisdictional anchor' that automatically extends to post-arbitration proceedings without independent grounding. The First Judiciary Act of 1789 and early federal practice reflect that federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction requiring affirmative statutory grants, and a stay — which merely suspends active litigation — cannot transmute into an indefinite reservoir of jurisdiction untethered from any statutory basis. While supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) may provide a viable pathway in some circumstances, the proper resolution consistent with Badgerow's textualist framework requires that jurisdiction be independently established rather than assumed from the mere existence of a prior stayed proceeding.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I find that 9 U.S.C. § 3 expressly contemplates that a court staying proceedings pending arbitration retains the case on its docket, and the plain text of the FAA does not require parties to re-establish jurisdictional grounds once a court has properly exercised original jurisdiction over the underlying dispute. The practical consequences of the Second Circuit's approach are deeply troubling from a law enforcement and judicial efficiency standpoint: requiring parties to identify a new independent jurisdictional basis post-arbitration would create the precisely the kind of bewildering two-track federal-state litigation scheme that Congress could not have intended when it enacted the FAA. Badgerow v. Walters, 596 U.S. 1 (2022), is distinguishable on its face because it addressed standalone applications to confirm or vacate awards filed as independent actions, not post-arbitration motions in a case that was continuously pending before the federal court under an established jurisdictional grant. The better reading of the statutory scheme is that a § 3 stay preserves the court's jurisdiction over the entire proceeding, including post-arbitration motions, because the case never left the federal docket and no new jurisdictional hook is required where original jurisdiction was properly established at the outset.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: When a federal court properly establishes subject matter jurisdiction over a case and stays it pending arbitration under FAA Section 3, that jurisdictional anchor persists throughout the pendency of the stayed proceeding, allowing the court to adjudicate post-arbitration motions without requiring a redundant independent jurisdictional basis. The Supreme Court's decision in Smith v. Spizzirri, 601 U.S. 472, 478 (2024), explicitly recognized that federal courts retain a 'supervisory role' over stayed arbitration proceedings that includes 'facilitating recovery on an arbitral award,' which would be rendered meaningless if parties were forced to file entirely new actions to confirm or vacate awards. Requiring a new independent jurisdictional basis for post-arbitration motions in an already-pending stayed case would impose severe practical burdens on vulnerable, often pro se litigants like Petitioner Jules, forcing duplicative litigation and creating perverse forum-shopping incentives that Congress could not have intended when it authorized stays rather than dismissals under the FAA. The supplemental jurisdiction statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a), further supports this conclusion, as post-arbitration motions in a stayed case are so related to the original claims that they form part of the same case or controversy, and the liberal construction owed to pro se litigants under Publicola v. Lomenzo reinforces that procedural technicalities should not foreclose access to justice here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: When a federal court properly establishes original jurisdiction and issues a stay under FAA Section 3, the case remains pending before that court — the stay is a procedural mechanism to pause proceedings, not a jurisdictional divestiture. The text and structure of the FAA, read alongside 28 U.S.C. § 1331, support the conclusion that jurisdiction attaches to the case, not merely to discrete motions within it, and a stayed case is still a live case. The Second Circuit's own pre-Badgerow doctrine, as reflected in Smiga v. Dean Witter Reynolds, correctly recognized that a court ordering arbitration retains jurisdiction over subsequent applications involving the same arbitration agreement — and Badgerow is distinguishable because it addressed freestanding post-arbitration petitions filed without any predicate federal case. Adopting Respondents' position would produce the exact kind of unworkable, two-track jurisdictional chaos — with parties potentially bouncing between federal and state court across the life of a single dispute — that Congress could not plausibly have intended when it mandated stays rather than dismissals, as confirmed by Smith v. Spizzirri (2024).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: As a textualist, I begin with the plain meaning of 9 U.S.C. § 3, which directs a court to 'stay the trial of the action' pending arbitration — the action remains pending before the court, not dismissed. Smith v. Spizzirri, 601 U.S. 472 (2024) confirmed that a stay under § 3 is mandatory and preserves the case on the court's docket, which strongly implies the court retains jurisdiction over that pending case to resolve post-arbitration motions without requiring a new independent jurisdictional basis. Kokkonen's ancillary jurisdiction doctrine further supports this conclusion: where a court retains a case on its docket and the post-arbitration motions are 'entwined' with the original proceeding, the court's ancillary power to enforce the resolution of that pending matter is well within traditional jurisdictional principles, as the research confirms. Requiring a new independent jurisdictional basis for post-arbitration motions in a stayed — not dismissed — case would contradict the plain statutory text, create perverse incentives to file duplicative federal actions, and undermine the structural logic of the FAA's integrated framework of §§ 3, 9, and 10.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The text of the FAA, as interpreted in Badgerow v. Walters, draws a meaningful distinction between Section 4 (which permits look-through jurisdiction) and Sections 9 and 10 (which do not), and that textual distinction strongly suggests Congress did not intend a stayed case to serve as a perpetual jurisdictional anchor for post-arbitration confirmation and vacatur proceedings. While I am sympathetic to the practical efficiency arguments Petitioner raises — and the concern about bewildering two-track litigation is real — the institutionalist in me recognizes that Congress expressly provided a maritime exception for the jurisdictional-anchor doctrine, and courts should respect that legislative judgment rather than judicially engineer a broader general rule. The circuit split, while present, remains shallow and insufficiently developed, and further percolation would sharpen the legal question and produce better-reasoned lower court opinions before this Court intervenes. Additionally, the vehicle concerns here — including the unpublished Second Circuit decision and the alternative pleading complications — counsel restraint, consistent with my general preference for deciding major jurisdictional questions in cleaner cases.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of FAA Section 3 directs a court to 'stay the trial of the action until such arbitration has been had,' which presupposes the action remains pending before that court throughout the arbitration — the stay preserves the case as a live federal proceeding, not merely a dormant one. Badgerow v. Williams, 596 U.S. 1 (2022), is distinguishable on its face because it addressed a freestanding petition to confirm or vacate filed as a new action, whereas here the post-arbitration motions arise within the same stayed case over which the district court already established original jurisdiction. Requiring parties to independently re-establish jurisdiction for post-arbitration motions in a stayed case would contradict the ordinary understanding that a court retaining a case on its docket retains jurisdiction over all proceedings in that case, and would produce the textually unsupported and practically incoherent two-track litigation scheme the research materials identify — including the anomaly that courts unquestionably retain jurisdiction over mid-arbitration motions under Sections 5 and 7 but would somehow lose it upon award issuance. Methodological consistency demands that the jurisdictional vessel created by the original filing and stay not be treated as having evaporated at the precise moment the arbitration concludes and the court's supervisory role becomes most consequential.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: When a federal court properly establishes original jurisdiction and stays a case pending arbitration under FAA Section 3, that stayed action remains a live, pending case on the court's docket — the jurisdictional foundation does not evaporate merely because the parties are directed to arbitrate. Badgerow v. Walters, 596 U.S. 1 (2022), is distinguishable on its face because it addressed freestanding applications to confirm or vacate filed as new actions, not post-arbitration motions filed within a previously-stayed federal proceeding; the Court itself noted this distinction. From a procedural fairness standpoint, requiring parties to independently re-establish jurisdiction for post-arbitration motions in the very same pending case would impose a formalistic and practically burdensome hurdle that undermines the FAA's efficiency goals and disproportionately harms pro se litigants like Petitioner Jules, who deserve the special solicitude recognized in Kotler v. Jubert and Publicola v. Lomenzo. The continuous jurisdiction approach better serves the practical consequences of the statutory scheme — Congress enacted Section 3 stays to preserve, not suspend, the federal court's supervisory role over the arbitration it compelled.

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable consensus, and I find the collective reasoning reinforces rather than undermines my position. Justice Alito's movement toward the petitioner — the colleague whose textualist objections I took most seriously — confirms that the stay/dismissal distinction is not merely a policy preference but reflects genuine legal consequences that even a rigorous textualist must acknowledge. I am gratified that my preferred narrow holding — limiting the jurisdictional anchor theory strictly to post-arbitration motions filed within a continuously pending stayed proceeding, leaving Badgerow fully intact for freestanding applications — has attracted broad support across methodological lines, from Justice Thomas's originalism to Justice Jackson's structural analysis. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with instructions to write narrowly on these grounds, avoiding any broad pronouncements about ancillary jurisdiction that could unsettle adjacent areas of law, and I would ensure the opinion explicitly cabins its holding to the § 3 stay context confirmed by Smith v. Spizzirri.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch raise the most serious challenge to my position by invoking Badgerow's textualist logic — that §§ 9 and 10 contain no look-through language and therefore require independent jurisdictional bases on the face of the application. But this argument, while textually serious, conflates two distinct questions: whether a freestanding post-arbitration application requires independent jurisdiction (Badgerow's holding), and whether a post-arbitration motion filed within a continuously pending stayed federal proceeding requires a fresh jurisdictional predicate. The original public meaning of Article III's 'Cases' and 'Controversies' language, combined with the First Congress's understanding of continuous judicial jurisdiction over pending actions, supports the view that a stayed case never ceased to be a 'Case' before the federal court — the stay is a procedural mechanism within the case, not a termination of it. Justice Gorsuch's concern that the 'jurisdictional anchor' theory bootstraps original jurisdiction into perpetual coverage is answered by the critical limiting principle: this theory applies only where the original case was stayed rather than dismissed, preserving the live proceeding, which is precisely the structural distinction that Smith v. Spizzirri confirms Congress intended to be meaningful.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: After careful reflection on my colleagues' arguments, I find Justice Barrett's point most persuasive: the expressio unius concern I raised regarding § 8's explicit 'retain jurisdiction' language is better understood as an affirmative grant in the admiralty context rather than a negative implication that retention is categorically unavailable elsewhere. The critical distinction — which Justice Roberts, Justice Gorsuch, and Justice Kagan all articulate with force — is that Badgerow addressed the threshold invocation of jurisdiction for a freestanding application, not the continuation of jurisdiction over a pending, stayed proceeding that was never dismissed. As a textualist, I must acknowledge that nothing in §§ 9 or 10 affirmatively strips a court of jurisdiction it already possesses; the absence of look-through language means those sections don't independently create jurisdiction, not that they destroy existing jurisdiction over a live docket entry. Smith v. Spizzirri's confirmation that stays are mandatory and preserve the proceeding — rather than terminating it — provides the structural anchor that distinguishes this case from Badgerow and justifies a narrow holding limited to stayed proceedings.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the strongest counterargument — that Badgerow's reasoning about the absence of look-through language in §§ 9 and 10 applies equally whether the post-arbitration motion arises in a stayed case or a freestanding application. But this argument proves too much: Badgerow addressed a petition filed for the first time post-arbitration with no prior federal proceeding, and its holding was explicitly cabined to that context. The jurisdictional anchor theory does not 'look through' the FAA application to manufacture jurisdiction from thin air — it recognizes that jurisdiction was properly and continuously invoked when the original federal case was filed and never terminated by dismissal. Justice Gorsuch's textualist concern about §§ 9 and 10's venue language is thoughtful, but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, reading the FAA as a coherent whole, Congress designed a single-forum framework for the entire dispute lifecycle, and the stay mechanism under § 3 — confirmed by Smith v. Spizzirri — reflects Congress's intent that the original court retain supervisory authority, making the Second Circuit's rule an anomaly that burdens exactly the vulnerable workers and less-resourced litigants who most need efficient access to federal courts.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito's movement toward the Petitioner position in Round 2 is significant precisely because he began as the most serious textualist skeptic, and his acknowledgment that the stay/dismissal distinction reflects actual legal consequences Congress attached to distinct procedural mechanisms — not merely policy preference — validates the core of my analysis. The unanimous convergence across methodological lines (Justice Thomas's originalism, Justice Gorsuch's textualism, Justice Sotomayor's purposivism, and my own pragmatic textualism) on the same structural distinction reinforces that this is not a coalition of convenience but a conclusion the FAA's text and structure genuinely compel. I continue to find Justice Alito's original expressio unius concern about § 8's explicit 'retain jurisdiction' language the most textually serious challenge, but Justice Barrett's response — that § 8 is an affirmative grant in the admiralty context rather than a negative implication foreclosing retention elsewhere — is the correct reading because treating § 8 as implicitly prohibiting retention in stayed proceedings would require reading a jurisdictional termination clause into silence, which is precisely the kind of inference the text cannot bear. The narrow holding I would craft — jurisdiction over post-arbitration motions filed within a continuously pending stayed proceeding requires no fresh predicate, while Badgerow governs freestanding applications — preserves doctrinal coherence, respects the stay/dismissal distinction Smith v. Spizzirri confirms is meaningful, and avoids the perverse incentive Justice Jackson correctly identifies of rewarding dismissal over stay.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the strongest counterargument from a textualist perspective — that Badgerow's logic, which found no look-through language in §§ 9 and 10, should apply equally here because those sections still contain no textual hook for retained jurisdiction. But I find this unpersuasive for a reason Justice Barrett identifies: the question in Badgerow was whether a freestanding post-arbitration application could look through to an underlying dispute to manufacture jurisdiction, whereas here the question is whether a court that already possesses jurisdiction over a pending, stayed proceeding must re-establish that jurisdiction at a later stage of the same case. These are categorically different questions — Badgerow addressed the threshold invocation of jurisdiction, not its continuation. The text of § 3, as Justice Kagan notes, contemplates a stay that preserves the proceeding rather than terminating it, and nothing in §§ 9 or 10 affirmatively strips a court of jurisdiction it already possesses over a pending case; the absence of look-through language in those sections simply means they don't independently create jurisdiction, not that they destroy existing jurisdiction. Justice Thomas's point about the historical understanding of Article III jurisdiction as continuous once properly invoked further reinforces that requiring a fresh jurisdictional predicate mid-proceeding lacks any textual or historical foundation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: After reviewing my colleagues' arguments in round two, I am more confident in the Petitioner's position. Justice Alito's movement toward Petitioner — despite his textualist instincts — is particularly significant: if the strongest textualist voice on the Court finds the stay/dismissal distinction legally meaningful rather than merely a policy preference, that confirms the distinction has genuine doctrinal grounding. Justice Barrett's point about § 8's explicit retention language being an affirmative grant rather than a negative implication continues to address my expressio unius concern most directly — § 8 operates in the admiralty context as an independent jurisdictional provision, not as the exclusive model for retention, and its presence does not imply that retention is unavailable when a § 3 stay preserves a live proceeding. The convergence across methodologies — Justice Thomas's originalist analysis, Justice Kagan's statutory coherence approach, and Justice Gorsuch's textualist reading — all reaching the same conclusion reinforces that this is not a result-oriented holding but one grounded in the FAA's structure as confirmed by Smith v. Spizzirri. My institutionalist concern about a narrow, principled holding is well-served by Chief Justice Roberts's framing: limit the rule to post-arbitration motions filed within a stayed, continuously pending federal docket, leaving Badgerow fully intact for freestanding applications.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: After reviewing my colleagues' arguments in round 2, I find the conference has converged on a principled distinction that I find textually and doctrinally sound. Justice Alito's movement toward the Petitioner position is particularly significant — as the justice who most rigorously pressed the Badgerow textualist argument, his acknowledgment that a stayed proceeding is categorically different from a freestanding application reflects the strength of the stay/dismissal distinction. Justice Gorsuch's reformulation is especially clarifying from a textualist standpoint: the absence of look-through language in §§ 9 and 10 means those sections don't independently create jurisdiction, not that they affirmatively destroy jurisdiction already properly invoked over a pending case — this is the correct reading because a negative inference from silence cannot bear the weight of stripping a court of jurisdiction it already possesses. I remain attentive to the expressio unius concern raised by § 8's explicit 'retain jurisdiction' language, but as I noted in round 1, § 8 is better understood as an affirmative grant in the admiralty context addressing a specific procedural circumstance, not as Congress's exclusive mechanism for retention — reading it otherwise would require courts to find implied jurisdictional terminations in the absence of any affirmative stripping language, which inverts the normal presumption. My confidence increases modestly because the unanimous conference position, reached through genuine engagement with the strongest counterarguments rather than mere coalition-building, reflects that the jurisdictional anchor theory for stayed proceedings is legally sound and appropriately narrow.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The deliberation has sharpened my confidence in the Petitioner's position. Justice Alito's movement toward Petitioner — despite his textualist commitments — is particularly significant: if the strongest textualist objection yields to the stayed-case distinction, that distinction is doing real legal work, not merely policy work. Justice Gorsuch's formulation is the one I find most clarifying: the absence of look-through language in §§ 9 and 10 means those provisions don't independently create jurisdiction, not that they destroy jurisdiction already properly invoked over a pending stayed case — these are categorically different questions, and Badgerow answered only the first. My background as a public defender reinforces what the structural analysis confirms: the FAA's stay mechanism, now mandatory under Smith v. Spizzirri, reflects a congressional choice to preserve continuous federal court involvement, and requiring less-resourced litigants to manufacture a fresh jurisdictional predicate mid-proceeding would impose asymmetric burdens that the statute's structure does not demand and that would perversely incentivize dismissal over stay.

John Roberts.reasoning: When a federal court exercises original jurisdiction over a case and stays it pursuant to 9 U.S.C. § 3 pending arbitration, the case remains a live, pending proceeding before that court — the stay does not extinguish jurisdiction but merely suspends active litigation. As this Court recognized in Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co., 511 U.S. 375 (1994), ancillary jurisdiction permits courts to enforce settlements and related matters arising from proceedings over which they already exercised jurisdiction, and the FAA's stay mechanism under § 3 — as recently confirmed in Smith v. Spizzirri, 601 U.S. 472 (2024) — contemplates exactly this kind of retained judicial supervision. The narrow, institutionally cautious resolution here is to hold that a court need not identify a new, independent jurisdictional basis when the original case was never dismissed and the post-arbitration motions are directly entwined with that pending proceeding, consistent with Peacock v. Thomas, 516 U.S. 349 (1996). I would distinguish Badgerow v. Walker, 596 U.S. 1 (2022), which addressed freestanding FAA applications filed without any underlying federal lawsuit, and decline to extend its holding to the materially different circumstance of a stayed but continuously pending federal case.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: From an originalist and textualist standpoint, Article III vests judicial power in federal courts over 'Cases' and 'Controversies,' and the First Congress understood jurisdiction over a case as continuous once properly invoked — there is no historical basis for requiring a fresh jurisdictional predicate at each procedural stage of the same pending action. The text of 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) further confirms this reading: once a district court has original jurisdiction, it possesses supplemental jurisdiction over all claims forming part of 'the same case or controversy,' and post-arbitration motions to confirm or vacate an award are not new cases but are integral resolutions of the original dispute. The Second Circuit's rule requiring an independent jurisdictional basis post-arbitration lacks any textual or historical foundation and imposes a judge-made requirement that neither Article III nor any statute demands. The circuit conflict, while perhaps not perfectly developed, presents a sufficiently recurring and consequential question of federal jurisdiction that warrants this Court's resolution to prevent forum-shopping and jurisdictional uncertainty across the circuits.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I am compelled to follow the Court's reasoning in Badgerow v. Walker, which held that Sections 9 and 10 of the FAA contain no look-through language and require an independent jurisdictional basis on the face of the application itself. The research materials confirm that neither Section 3's stay provision nor Section 4's compel-arbitration provision contains any textual hook supporting a 'jurisdictional anchor' theory that would automatically extend original jurisdiction to post-arbitration motions. Adopting petitioner's position would effectively redline the FAA by importing jurisdictional language into Sections 9 and 10 that Congress deliberately omitted, as the Court warned against in Badgerow. While I recognize the practical appeal of petitioner's argument that a stayed case remains a pending proceeding, the absence of any statutory text supporting retained jurisdiction in this context is dispositive under proper textualist analysis, and the circuit split respondents characterize as shallow counsels against granting certiorari on an insufficiently developed record.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: When a federal court stays a case pending arbitration rather than dismissing it, the court retains the original jurisdictional hook that brought the parties before it, and requiring a new independent basis for subject matter jurisdiction to hear post-arbitration motions in that same pending proceeding elevates form over substance in a way that burdens vulnerable litigants and creates needless inefficiency. The Supreme Court's recent decision in Smith v. Spizzirri, 601 U.S. 472 (2024), confirms that federal courts have a supervisory role that includes facilitating recovery on an arbitral award, strongly suggesting that a stayed case preserves the court's authority to act on post-arbitration motions. Section 1367(a)'s supplemental jurisdiction provision further supports this conclusion, as post-arbitration motions to confirm or vacate an award arise from the same case or controversy that originally vested the court with jurisdiction, and the doctrine of ancillary jurisdiction has long allowed courts to resolve related matters in pending proceedings without demanding a duplicative jurisdictional basis. The Second Circuit's contrary rule creates a perverse incentive where parties who successfully obtain a stay face greater jurisdictional hurdles than those whose cases were dismissed, disproportionately harming workers and other less-resourced litigants who cannot easily file new federal actions.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text and structure of 9 U.S.C. § 3 strongly support petitioner's position: a stay 'preserves' rather than terminates federal jurisdiction, and the stayed case remains a continuously pending proceeding throughout arbitration. Reading §§ 3, 9, and 10 as a coherent statutory framework, Congress designed the FAA to allow a single federal forum to manage the entire dispute lifecycle—compelling arbitration, staying proceedings, and then adjudicating post-arbitration motions—without forcing parties to identify a new jurisdictional hook after the stay lifts. The respondents' contrary reading produces the kind of bewildering two-track, forum-splitting inefficiency that Congress plainly did not intend, requiring parties to simultaneously pursue federal appeals of pre-arbitration orders while litigating confirmation or vacatur in state court. While Badgerow correctly held that freestanding post-arbitration applications require independent jurisdiction, that holding is distinguishable because it addressed petitions filed for the first time post-arbitration, not motions filed within a continuously pending stayed federal action where original jurisdiction was never relinquished.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of 9 U.S.C. §§ 9 and 10 requires an independent jurisdictional basis for confirmation and vacatur applications, and nothing in the FAA's structure suggests that a prior stay under § 3 transforms those discrete post-arbitration applications into mere continuations of the original proceeding for jurisdictional purposes. The Court's reasoning in Badgerow v. Walter made clear that federal courts cannot look through FAA applications to underlying disputes to manufacture jurisdiction, and the 'jurisdictional anchor' theory effectively does exactly that by bootstrapping the original complaint's federal claims into perpetual jurisdictional coverage over what are, textually, separate statutory applications. As a textualist, I am skeptical of judge-made doctrines like ancillary jurisdiction that expand federal court power beyond what Congress has authorized, particularly where, as here, the statutory text of §§ 9 and 10 is addressed to 'the United States court in and for the district' where the award was made — language that speaks to venue and filing, not to the perpetuation of a prior court's jurisdiction. The circuit split is real and acknowledged, the question is recurring and important, and the Second Circuit's approach provides a roadmap for parties to evade Badgerow simply by filing a federal lawsuit first, which cannot be what Congress intended.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: When a federal court exercises original jurisdiction over a case and stays it pending arbitration under Section 3 of the FAA rather than dismissing it, the case remains a live, pending proceeding before that court, and established principles of ancillary and supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) support the court's authority to resolve post-arbitration motions without requiring a duplicative independent jurisdictional basis. The critical practical distinction between a stay and a dismissal is well-grounded in our precedents and reflects a meaningful structural choice — a stay preserves the court's continuing supervisory role over the proceeding, while a dismissal terminates it, and treating these identically would undermine the FAA's coherent framework for judicial enforcement of arbitration awards. While Badgerow v. Walters correctly held that Sections 9 and 10 applications filed as standalone matters require an independent jurisdictional basis, that holding's logic is cabined to cases where no prior federal proceeding exists, and extending it to stayed cases would create perverse incentives for parties to forum-shop by strategically choosing dismissal over stay to defeat federal jurisdiction. The practical workability concerns here are real, not speculative — requiring litigants who properly invoked federal jurisdiction at the outset to re-establish it post-arbitration imposes unnecessary burdens and risks inconsistent outcomes that undermine the Court's institutional credibility.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: As a textualist and originalist, I find the FAA's structure and the Court's decision in Smith v. Spizzirri (601 U.S. 478) instructive: when a court stays a case under 9 U.S.C. § 3 rather than dismissing it, the proceeding remains pending before that court, and the original jurisdictional basis does not evaporate during the stay. The Second Circuit's requirement of a new, independent jurisdictional basis for post-arbitration motions in the same stayed proceeding conflates the question of whether jurisdiction was properly established at the outset with whether it must be re-established—a distinction unsupported by the FAA's text or the historical understanding of ancillary jurisdiction as articulated in Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co., 511 U.S. 375 (1994), and Peacock v. Thomas, 516 U.S. 349 (1996). While Section 8's explicit 'retain jurisdiction' language does give me pause under the expressio unius canon, the better reading is that Section 8 creates an affirmative grant in the admiralty context rather than implying that retention is categorically unavailable elsewhere, particularly where a stay—not a dismissal—preserves the live proceeding. The circuit conflict, though arguably shallow, presents a sufficiently recurring and important jurisdictional question under the FAA to warrant this Court's resolution.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: When a federal court with original jurisdiction stays a case under 9 U.S.C. § 3 pending arbitration, the underlying civil action remains pending before that court — the stay preserves rather than extinguishes jurisdiction. Requiring parties to identify a new, independent jurisdictional basis for post-arbitration motions in the same proceeding elevates formalism over practical reality, creates perverse incentives for forum-shopping, and imposes procedural burdens that fall disproportionately on less-resourced litigants — concerns that resonate deeply with my background as a public defender attentive to how procedural rules operate in practice. The 'jurisdictional anchor' theory adopted by the Fifth and Eleventh Circuits reflects the better reading of § 3's text and structure: once the court's jurisdiction is properly invoked and the case is stayed rather than dismissed, the court retains continuous jurisdiction over the proceeding, including post-arbitration motions to confirm or vacate under §§ 9-10, without requiring a fresh jurisdictional hook. The Second Circuit's contrary rule, as illustrated in Smarter Tools and Beijing Shougang, creates an anomalous and unworkable framework that undermines the FAA's purpose of efficient dispute resolution.
